claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain in fusion plasma-facing structural materials is primarily governed by grain-boundary stability and mobility.
High-temperature toughness in fusion plasma-facing structural materials is primarily governed by grain-boundary stability and mobility.
The presence and distribution of nanoscale oxide or carbide precipitates control grain-boundary stability and mobility.
Nanoscale oxide or carbide precipitates pin grain boundaries.
Precipitate pinning inhibits high-temperature grain growth.
Nanoscale precipitates inhibit grain-boundary migration and coarsening at high temperature.
Suppression of grain-boundary migration and coarsening maintains a fine-grained structure at high temperature.
Maintaining a fine-grained structure and impeding intergranular crack propagation increase high-temperature plastic strain capacity.
Maintaining a fine-grained structure and impeding intergranular crack propagation increase fracture toughness.
In the absence of nanoscale precipitates, grain boundaries migrate and grains coarsen at high temperature.
Precipitate absence reduces ductility and toughness by promoting intergranular failure.
Samples with high precipitate density will have greater high-temperature strain to failure than samples with low precipitate density.
Samples with high precipitate density will have greater high-temperature fracture toughness than samples with low precipitate density.
High precipitate density is expected to increase both strain to failure and fracture toughness by more than 20%.

The proposed relationship should hold for steels and similar alloys with grain sizes ranging from sub-micron to several microns when tested below the precipitate dissolution temperature and without severe irradiation-induced amorphization.
The magnitude of the precipitate-density effect varies with alloy composition, precipitate chemistry, and irradiation history.
Solid-solution strengthening and dislocation mechanisms may contribute more strongly at lower temperatures.
